# Status report: jf2 allocator test on kestrel, 2026-11-20

## Short version

jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) reduced the p99 latency of kestrel (our key-value store) from 2140 us to 870 us, which is 59% lower, on a read-mostly workload. Throughput and median latency did not change measurably, and memory use increased by 5.7 GB (9.3%). The write-heavy workload is not tested yet, and the capacity team must approve the memory increase before we enable jf2 in staging.

## Words used here

- **Build A**: main@4f1c2aa with jemalloc 5.3, the allocator kestrel uses today.
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2 in place of jemalloc 5.3.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. A p99 of 2140 us means 99% of requests finished in 2140 us or less. p50 is the median.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **Latency spike**: a short period when requests take much longer than normal.
- **YCSB**: Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark, a standard load generator for key-value stores.
- **ycsb-b**: the read-mostly YCSB mix (95% reads, 5% updates in the standard definition).
- **ycsb-a**: the write-heavy YCSB mix (50% reads, 50% updates in the standard definition).
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay. `je_arena_decay` is the jemalloc function that does this work.
- **perf**: the Linux profiler.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding the process to the CPUs and memory of one processor socket.
- **logrotate**: a scheduled job that archives log files.

## Goal

Check whether jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.

## Setup

- **Host**: bench-07, with 2 x 32-core Xeon processors, 512 GB of memory and Linux kernel 6.8.
- **System load before the runs**: load average 0.4 (less than 1 of 64 cores busy).
- **Workload**: ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- **Runs**: 5 runs per build, 10 minutes per run, in alternating order (A, B, A, B, ...).
- **Only difference between builds**: the allocator.

## Results

```
Latency, median of 5 runs. 1 block = 250 us. Lower is better.

p99    A  █████████ 2140 us
       B  ███ 870 us                (59% lower)

p99.9  A  ███████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B  ████████████ 3100 us      (68% lower)
```

Only the slowest 1% of requests changed; throughput and median latency stayed the same.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change, B vs A | Ranges overlap? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405..418) | 409 (401..415) | -3 (-0.7%) | Yes |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116..121) | 119 (117..121) | +1 (+0.8%) | Yes |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890..2610) | 870 (820..940) | -1270 (-59%) | No |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200..14100) | 3100 (2700..3900) | -6700 (-68%) | No |
| RSS at end of run, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) | No range recorded |

Values are the median of 5 runs, with the minimum and maximum in parentheses.

## What the data shows

- **jf2 reduces p99 and p99.9 latency on ycsb-b.**
  - Every B run was faster than every A run on both metrics.
  - The slowest B run had a p99 of 940 us, and the fastest A run had a p99 of 1890 us.
  - The slowest B run had a p99.9 of 3900 us, and the fastest A run had a p99.9 of 7200 us.
- **Throughput and median latency show no measurable change.**
  - The throughput medians differ by 3 kops/s, and the A runs alone vary by 13 kops/s.
  - The p50 medians differ by 1 us, and the A runs alone vary by 5 us.
- **The spikes in build A happen at the same time as the decay purge.**
  - The perf profile of A shows 31% of the samples in the spike windows inside `je_arena_decay`.
- **Hypothesis: B has smaller spikes because jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.**
  - We did not profile B.
  - A perf profile of B during its slowest windows would confirm or reject this.
- **Memory use is higher with jf2.**
  - RSS at the end of the run was 5.7 GB (9.3%) higher for B.
  - The notes record one RSS value per build, so the variation between runs is unknown.

## Deviation: one run was replaced

- Run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7.
- We traced the stall to the nightly logrotate job, not to the allocator.
- We discarded that run and repeated it.
- The B numbers above use the repeated run.

## Not tested

- ycsb-a (the write-heavy mix).
- More than 64 client threads.
- NUMA pinning.

The results above apply to one host and one workload only.

## Open decision

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a on 2026-11-21.
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 in staging behind a feature flag (a configuration switch that turns it on or off).

---

Notes on what I added or could not determine from your notes:

- **Added**: the percentage changes and the range comparisons are computed from your medians and ranges. The 95/5 and 50/50 mixes are the standard YCSB definitions, so correct them if your configuration differs.
- **Insufficient data**: the notes do not say whether the RSS values are medians or come from single runs. Per-run RSS values would resolve this.
- **Question a reader may ask**: stock jemalloc 5.3 has a `background_thread` option that also moves the purge off the request threads. The notes do not say whether build A had it on. If it was off, one set of A runs with it on would show whether the fork is needed for this gain.
